This vignette is the technical reference of `panglm`. It states the
models, the estimating equations and the covariance estimators, lists
the established implementations each estimator is validated against,
and defines the scope of the package. Worked examples are in the task
vignettes:

| Topic | Vignette |
|---|---|
| Data layout, pooled, within, between, random and correlated random effects, standard errors, partial effects, tables | `vignette("panglm-intro")` |
| Counts, hurdle, two-part costs, beta, ordered and tobit models | `vignette("panglm-outcomes")` |
| Instrumental variables, Hausman-Taylor, dynamic GMM, sample selection | `vignette("panglm-endogeneity")` |
| Difference-in-differences, event studies, staggered adoption | `vignette("panglm-policy")` |
| Random slopes, latent classes, quantile regression | `vignette("panglm-heterogeneity")` |

The numerical routines use Rcpp, RcppArmadillo and RcppParallel.

```{r setup}
library(panglm)
data(copd)
```

## Notation and data organization

Let $y_{it}$ be the response of unit $i = 1, \dots, N$ at occasion
$t = 1, \dots, T_i$, and $x_{it}$ a vector of covariates. The
conditional mean is linked to a linear predictor by

$$
g\{E(y_{it} \mid x_{it}, \alpha_i, \gamma_t)\}
= x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + \alpha_i + \gamma_t,
$$

where $\alpha_i$ is an individual effect and $\gamma_t$ an optional time
effect. `index` names the individual and time variables. `model` sets
how $\alpha_i$ is treated:

* `"pooling"` omits $\alpha_i$;
* `"within"` treats $\alpha_i$ as a fixed nuisance parameter;
* `"between"` regresses individual means on individual means;
* `"random"` gives $\alpha_i$ a distribution and integrates it out.

`effect = "twoways"` adds the time effects to supported fixed-effects
models.

Model matrices follow the usual R formula rules. Before estimation the
rank is checked after the transformation of the requested estimator;
unidentified columns, such as time-invariant regressors in a within
model, are reported and dropped. Missing responses or covariates follow
`na.action`; missing or duplicated index pairs are errors. Nonzero
offsets are rejected. Observation weights are accepted by pooled models
and, when constant within individuals, by random-effects models.

## Linear estimators

**Pooled.** Least squares, or iteratively reweighted least squares
(IRLS) for generalized linear models. The negative binomial model uses
the NB2 variance $\mu_{it} + \mu_{it}^2/\theta$ and alternates
coefficient updates with the estimation of $\theta$. With prior weights
$w_{it}$ the score is $\sum_{it} w_{it} s_{it}(\beta)$; zero weights
remove an observation from the fit, the likelihood and the degrees of
freedom. Robust and cluster covariances use the weighted scores and
treat the weights as known, which is the usual inverse probability
weighting for attrition.

**Within.** The one-way estimator is least squares on
$\tilde y_{it} = y_{it} - \bar y_i$ and
$\tilde x_{it} = x_{it} - \bar x_i$. With `effect = "twoways"`
alternating projections remove both individual and time means, which
also handles unbalanced panels.

**Between.** Least squares on the individual means,
$\bar y_i = \bar x_i^{\mathsf T}\beta + \bar u_i$, one row per
individual. Its HC1 covariance equals the cluster covariance because
each individual contributes one row.

**Random effects.** The Gaussian model is the Swamy and Arora (1972)
feasible GLS estimator: with
$\lambda_i = 1 - \sigma_\varepsilon / (\sigma_\varepsilon^2 + T_i\sigma_\alpha^2)^{1/2}$
it regresses $y_{it} - \lambda_i \bar y_i$ on
$x_{it} - \lambda_i \bar x_i$, with variance components from the within
and between residuals. In a balanced panel
$\hat\sigma_\alpha^2 = s_b^2 - \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 / T$ with $s_b^2$ the
residual variance of the between regression. In an unbalanced panel the
between regression weights each individual by $T_i$ and the variance
components solve the trace-based moment equations of `plm`
(`random.method = "swar"`), which reduce to the balanced ones when all
$T_i$ are equal. A negative $\hat\sigma_\alpha^2$ is set to zero with a
warning. With weights, or with random slopes, the Gaussian model is
fitted by maximum likelihood instead.

## Nonlinear fixed effects

**Poisson.** For one-way models the individual intercept has the
closed-form profile solution
$\hat\alpha_i(\beta) = \log\{Y_i / L_i(\beta)\}$, with
$Y_i = \sum_t y_{it}$ and $L_i(\beta) = \sum_t \exp(x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta)$.
Substitution gives the conditional Poisson estimator (Hausman, Hall and
Griliches 1984), which is consistent for fixed $T$ when the conditional
mean is correct. Two-way models use an outer IRLS loop with weighted
alternating projections (Guimaraes and Portugal 2010).

**Negative binomial.** The one-way NB2 model estimates the slopes, one
intercept per individual and $\theta$ jointly (Allison and Waterman
2002); all-zero groups are dropped with a message. It is not the
conditional negative binomial model of Hausman, Hall and Griliches
(1984), whose scale restriction does not remove an individual
intercept. Dummy intercepts do not remove the finite-$T$ incidental
parameter bias in general, so short panels call for caution.

**Gamma.** With $E(y_{it} \mid x_{it}, \alpha_i) =
\exp(\alpha_i + x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta)$ the gamma log-link estimator
with one intercept per individual is consistent for fixed $T$ under
strict exogeneity, because its concentrated score has mean zero, as for
the Poisson model. The log-link working weights are constant, so each
IRLS step is a within regression.

**Binomial.** The one-way model is the exact conditional logit
(Chamberlain 1980). Given $S_i = \sum_t y_{it}$, unit $i$ contributes

$$
L_i(\beta \mid S_i) =
\frac{\exp\left(\sum_t y_{it}x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta\right)}
{\sum_{a:\,\sum_t a_t=S_i}
 \exp\left(\sum_t a_tx_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta\right)},
$$

evaluated with its score by a forward and backward recursion. Units with
all-zero or all-one responses carry no information and are dropped.
With `effect = "twoways"` the individual effects are conditioned out
and time effects enter as dummies.

**Ordered logit.** `model = "within"` fits the blow-up and cluster
estimator of Baetschmann, Staub and Winkelmann (2015): each observation
is copied once per cutoff, dichotomized at that cutoff, and a
conditional logit is fitted to the stacked data with standard errors
clustered by individual.

## Random-intercept likelihoods

Random-effects models integrate over $\alpha_i$:

| Family | Mixing distribution | Integration |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | normal | closed form (FGLS or ML) |
| Poisson | gamma | closed form (negative binomial marginal) |
| Negative binomial | beta on the NB2 probability | closed form (Hausman, Hall and Griliches 1984) |
| Binomial (logit, probit) | normal | Gauss-Hermite quadrature |
| Gamma, ordered, beta, tobit | normal on the link scale | adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature |

`R` sets the number of quadrature nodes. Adaptive quadrature centres the
nodes at each individual's mode and scales them by the curvature there;
`R = 1` is the Laplace approximation. Response predictions are marginal
over $\alpha_i$; for the gamma model this includes the lognormal factor
$\exp(\sigma_\alpha^2/2)$. Covariances use the observed information, and
`vcov = "cluster"` gives the sandwich built from the individual scores
of the integrated likelihood. With weights constant within individuals
the weighted sum of the individual log-likelihoods is maximized and the
cluster covariance is design based.

**Correlated random effects.** `cre = TRUE` adds the individual means
of the time-varying regressors, $\alpha_i = \bar x_i^{\mathsf T}\gamma +
a_i$ (Mundlak 1978; Chamberlain 1980), as `mean_<variable>` columns. In
linear models the coefficients on $x_{it}$ then equal the within
estimates. The summary reports the Wald test of $\gamma = 0$, the
regression form of the Hausman test.

**Dynamic models.** `dynamic = TRUE` applies the initial-conditions
solution of Wooldridge (2005): it adds the lagged outcome `lag_<y>`, the
first observed outcome `initial_<y>` and the individual means of the
time-varying regressors, and drops the first wave. The coefficient on
`lag_<y>` measures state dependence.

## Random slopes

`random = ~ z` gives the model
$g\{E(y_{it} \mid b_i)\} = x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + z_{it}^{\mathsf T}b_i$,
with $z_{it}$ the intercept and the listed variables and
$b_i \sim N(0, \Sigma)$, $\Sigma$ unstructured (Laird and Ware 1982).
The Gaussian model is fitted by exact maximum likelihood. Poisson,
negative binomial, gamma and binomial (logit or probit) models use
adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature on a product grid of $R^q$ nodes, with
$q$ the dimension of $b_i$; the cost therefore grows quickly with $q$.
$\Sigma$ is parametrized by its Cholesky factor. The fit stores
$\hat\Sigma$ in `varcomp` and the predicted effects (posterior modes, the
BLUPs in the Gaussian case) in `ranef`.

## Outcome-specific models

**Ordered.** `orderedfamily("logit")` or `orderedfamily("probit")`:
$P(y_{it} \le j) = F(c_j - x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta - \alpha_i)$, with the
intercept absorbed in the cutpoints $c_j$. Pooled and random-intercept
fits for both links; the fixed-effects model above for the logit link.

**Beta.** `betafamily()`: $y_{it} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\mu_{it}\phi,
(1 - \mu_{it})\phi)$ with $g(\mu_{it}) = x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta$, so
$\mathrm{Var}(y_{it}) = \mu_{it}(1 - \mu_{it})/(1 + \phi)$ (Ferrari and
Cribari-Neto 2004). The precision is `fit$precision`. Responses of
exactly 0 or 1 must first be moved inside the interval (Smithson and
Verkuilen 2006). Regressors should be on a moderate scale.

**Tobit.** `tobitfamily(left, right)`: a latent
$y^*_{it} = x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}$,
$\varepsilon_{it} \sim N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$, is observed as
$y_{it} = \min\{\max(y^*_{it}, \ell), r\}$ (Tobin 1958). Censored
observations contribute $\Phi\{(\ell - \eta_{it})/\sigma_\varepsilon\}$
or $1 - \Phi\{(r - \eta_{it})/\sigma_\varepsilon\}$, the others the
normal density. Pooled and random-intercept models; the random
intercept SD is `fit$sigma` and the error SD `fit$sigma_e`.

**Two-part.** `twopart()` fits the model of Duan et al. (1983),
$E(y_{it}) = P(y_{it} > 0)\, E(y_{it} \mid y_{it} > 0)$, with a probit or
logit first part and a gamma (log link) or lognormal positive part,
pooled or with random intercepts, optionally with `cre = TRUE`. The
lognormal retransformation uses Duan's smearing factor (default) or
$\exp(\sigma^2/2)$. With `correlated = TRUE` and a lognormal positive
part, the two random intercepts are bivariate normal with correlation
$\rho$ and both parts are fitted jointly (Van Ourti 2004). The positive
part integrates in closed form given $u_{1i}$, and the integral over
$u_{1i}$ uses adaptive quadrature. The marginal mean is then

$$
E(y_{it}) = \exp\{z_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + (\sigma_e^2 + \tau^2)/2\}\,
E_{u_1}\{F(x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\gamma + u_1)\, e^{c u_1}\},
\quad c = \rho\sigma_2/\sigma_1,\; \tau^2 = \sigma_2^2(1 - \rho^2).
$$

**Hurdle.** `panhurdle()` fits two fixed-effects parts: a conditional
logit for $1(y_{it} > 0)$ and a zero-truncated Poisson or NB2 model for
the positive counts, with density
$f(y \mid \mu, \theta)/\{1 - f(0 \mid \mu, \theta)\}$ for $y > 0$ and
one intercept per individual.

## Endogenous regressors

**Two-stage least squares.** `paniv()` takes `y ~ regressors |
instruments`, where the second part is the full instrument set. With
$\tilde a$ the within, quasi-demeaned or untransformed version of a
variable and $\hat X = P_{\tilde Z}\tilde X$,

$$
\hat\beta_{\mathrm{2SLS}} = (\hat X^{\mathsf T}\tilde X)^{-1}
\hat X^{\mathsf T}\tilde y .
$$

`model = "within"` and `"pooling"` give fixed-effects and pooled 2SLS.
`model = "random"` gives the generalized 2SLS of Balestra and
Varadharajan-Krishnakumar (`inst.method = "bvk"`) or the EC2SLS of
Baltagi (1981) (`"baltagi"`, instruments $[QZ, PZ]$), with variance
components from within and between 2SLS residuals. The summary reports
the first-stage partial $R^2$ and $F$ of the excluded instruments, and
a Sargan test (or a cluster-robust Hansen $J$) when overidentified.

**Hausman-Taylor.** `model = "hausmantaylor"` (Hausman and Taylor 1981)
splits the regressors into time-varying and time-invariant, exogenous
and endogenous with respect to $\alpha_i$. The second formula part lists
the exogenous ones. The within-transformed time-varying regressors and
the exogenous time-varying means and time-invariant regressors are the
instruments, so the exogenous time-varying regressors must be at least
as many as the endogenous time-invariant ones.

**Dynamic GMM.** `pangmm()` fits
$y_{it} = \rho y_{i,t-1} + x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + \alpha_i +
\varepsilon_{it}$. The difference estimator of Arellano and Bond (1991)
uses $E(y_{is}\Delta\varepsilon_{it}) = 0$ for $s \le t - 2$; the system
estimator of Blundell and Bond (1998) (`transformation = "ld"`) adds
$E(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\varepsilon_{it}) = 0$. `collapse = TRUE` and
`maxlag` limit the instrument count. The two-step covariance uses the
Windmeijer (2005) correction. Reported tests: Arellano-Bond AR(1) and
AR(2), Sargan and Hansen.

**Sample selection.** `panselect()` implements Wooldridge (1995). A
probit for selection is fitted in each period, with the individual
means of the selection regressors (`mundlak = TRUE`). The inverse Mills
ratio, interacted with period dummies (`lambda = "period"`) or common
(`"common"`), enters the outcome equation, estimated by fixed effects or
pooled OLS. The joint test of the Mills ratio terms is the test of
selection bias; it is valid with the cluster covariance under the null.
Coefficient standard errors come from a cluster bootstrap over both
steps (`boot` replicates).

## Policy evaluation

**Two-way fixed effects.** `did()` fits
$g\{E(y_{it})\} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \delta D_{it} +
x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta$, with $D_{it} = 1(t \ge g_i)$ and $g_i$ the
first treated period. Gaussian, Poisson, negative binomial and
conditional logit fits are available. Poisson TWFE needs only the
conditional mean to be correct (Wooldridge 2023). `eventstudy()`
replaces $D_{it}$ with indicators of event time $e = t - g_i$ from
`-leads` to `lags`, reference `ref = -1`, with the end points binned by
default. Its Wald test of the leads is the pre-trend test. Under
staggered adoption with heterogeneous effects the TWFE coefficient is a
weighted average of two-by-two comparisons with possibly negative
weights (Goodman-Bacon 2021; Sun and Abraham 2021).

**Group-time effects.** `attgt()` estimates, for each cohort $g$ and
period $t$,

$$
\mathrm{ATT}(g, t) = E(y_t - y_{b} \mid G = g) -
E(y_t - y_{b} \mid C),
$$

with base period $b = g - 1$ (moved back by `anticipation`) and
comparison group $C$ never or not yet treated (Callaway and Sant'Anna
2021). Pre-treatment ATT$(g, t)$ use the previous period as base
(`base = "varying"`) or $g - 1$ (`base = "universal"`). With covariates the
comparison is outcome regression, inverse probability weighting or the
doubly robust combination (Sant'Anna and Zhao 2020). Aggregations
(`summary(type = "simple", "dynamic", "group", "calendar")`) weight the
ATT$(g, t)$ by cohort size. Standard errors come from the influence
functions, or from the multiplier bootstrap (`bstrap`, `biters`), which
allows a coarser `cluster` and uniform bands (`cband`).

**Extended TWFE.** `etwfe()` (Wooldridge 2021, 2023) fits one pooled
regression with cohort and period effects and a treatment indicator for
every treated cohort by post-period cell; covariates enter centred at
their cohort means and interacted with the cells. In the linear case the cell coefficients
equal the imputation estimates of ATT$(g, t)$. With `family = "poisson"`
or `"binomial"` parallel trends holds on the link scale and the effects
are averaged on the response scale with delta-method standard errors.
`xvar` gives effects by a covariate; `ivar = TRUE` uses unit instead of
cohort effects (linear only).

## Finite mixtures

`panfmm()` assumes each individual belongs to one of $k$ latent classes
for all its observations, so the likelihood contribution is

$$
L_i = \sum_{c=1}^{k} \pi_c(w_i) \prod_t f_c(y_{it} \mid x_{it};
\beta_c), \qquad
\pi_c(w_i) = \frac{\exp(w_i^{\mathsf T}\delta_c)}{\sum_l
\exp(w_i^{\mathsf T}\delta_l)},
$$

with Gaussian, Poisson, NB2 or binomial components (Deb and Trivedi
1997, 2002) and individual-level concomitant variables $w_i$
(`concomitant`). EM is run from `nstart` random starts and the best fit
kept; the covariance is the inverse observed information of the full
likelihood, or its cluster sandwich. `panfmmselect()` compares
$k$ by AIC and BIC. `predict(type = "posterior")` returns the posterior
class probabilities.

## Quantile regression

`panqr()` assumes $Q_{y_{it}}(\tau \mid x_{it}, \alpha_i) = \alpha_i +
x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta(\tau)$ with location-shift individual effects.

* `"canay"` (Canay 2011): $\hat\alpha_i$ from the within regression, then
  `quantreg` regression of $y_{it} - \hat\alpha_i$ on $x_{it}$.
  Consistent as $N$ and $T$ grow. Analytic or cluster bootstrap
  standard errors.
* `"mmqr"` (Machado and Santos Silva 2019): the location-scale model
  $y_{it} = \alpha_i + x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + (\delta_i +
  x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\gamma)U_{it}$, estimated by two within regressions
  and the $\tau$-quantile $q(\tau)$ of the standardized residuals, so
  $\beta(\tau) = \beta + \gamma q(\tau)$. Analytic covariance as in
  their paper.
* `"pooling"`: `quantreg` regression ignoring $\alpha_i$, with a
  cluster-robust covariance.

## Regression splines

Any formula term works, including `splines::ns(x, df)`,
`splines::bs(x, df)` and `poly(x, degree)`. Basis columns are demeaned
like any regressor in fixed-effects fits, and the knots of the
estimation sample are reused by `predict()` and `model.matrix()`.

* `lineartest(fit, "x")`: the spline basis contains the linear function,
  $x = c + Ba$, so linearity means the spline coefficients are
  proportional to $a$; the test is the joint Wald test of the $q - 1$
  implied restrictions, with any covariance type.
* `jointtest(fit, pattern = "x")`: Wald test that all columns of `x` are
  zero.
* `effectcurve(fit, "x", ref)`: change in the linear predictor from
  `ref` to a grid of values, with delta-method pointwise limits.

```{r splines}
set.seed(2026)
N <- 150; TT <- 5
sim <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), year = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
alpha <- rnorm(N)
sim$bmi <- 27 + 3 * alpha[sim$id] + rnorm(N * TT, sd = 2.5)
sim$logcost <- 6 + alpha[sim$id] + 0.004 * (sim$bmi - 23)^2 +
  rnorm(N * TT, sd = 0.4)
fit_spline <- panglm(logcost ~ splines::ns(bmi, 4), data = sim,
                     index = c("id", "year"), model = "within",
                     vcov = "cluster")
lineartest(fit_spline, "bmi")
```

```{r splines-plot, fig.alt = "Within effect of BMI on log spending relative to BMI 25 with a pointwise band; the true curve is dashed"}
plot(effectcurve(fit_spline, "bmi", ref = 25), xlab = "Body mass index",
     ylab = "Change in log spending vs BMI 25")
curve(0.004 * (x - 23)^2 - 0.004 * (25 - 23)^2, add = TRUE, lty = 2)
```

A likelihood ratio test of nested fixed-effects fits is biased upwards
here: the dummy-variable error variance divides the residual sum of
squares by $NT$ instead of $N(T - 1)$, which inflates the statistic by
about $T/(T - 1)$. The Wald form is preferred.

## Average partial effects

`partialeffects()` averages
$\partial E(y_{it} \mid x_{it}) / \partial x_{itj}$ over the sample for
continuous regressors, and the discrete change for binary and factor
regressors, with delta-method standard errors from the stored
covariance. For random-effects models the mean integrates over
$\alpha_i$, the average structural function of Wooldridge (2005); in
correlated random effects fits the individual means are held fixed.
Ordered models give one effect per category; two-part models give
effects on either part or on the unconditional mean.

## Covariance estimation

The default covariance is model based. With $B$ the inverse information
and $s_j$ the score contributions, the sandwich is

$$
\hat V(\hat\beta) = B
\left(\sum_j s_j(\hat\beta)s_j(\hat\beta)^{\mathsf T}\right)B .
$$

`"HC1"` uses observation scores; `"cluster"` sums them within clusters
first, the individual by default or a coarser `cluster` variable. Linear
models use the finite-sample factor
$G/(G - 1) \cdot (n - 1)/(n - k)$ of `plm::vcovHC(type = "sss")`. For the
conditional logit the independent contribution is a whole stratum, so
HC1 uses stratum scores and a custom cluster may combine but not split
strata. For random-effects models the scores are those of the
individual integrated likelihoods.

```{r vcov}
fit_fe <- panglm(fev1 ~ crp, data = copd, index = c("id", "visit"),
                 model = "within")
sqrt(c(classical = vcov(fit_fe), HC1 = vcov(fit_fe, type = "HC1"),
       cluster = vcov(fit_fe, type = "cluster")))
```

`panhausman()` compares compatible fixed- and random-effects fits with
the covariance difference, or in its Mundlak form with any covariance.
`pandispersiontest()` reports the Pearson statistic over its residual
degrees of freedom for count fits.

## Likelihoods and information criteria

`logLik()`, `AIC()` and `BIC()` count the estimated shape, dispersion,
variance and absorbed fixed-effect parameters that belong to the
reported likelihood. Gaussian within fits report the dummy-variable
normal likelihood, and Swamy-Arora fits the exact (not REML) normal
random-intercept likelihood at the FGLS estimates. Conditional Poisson
and conditional logit likelihoods count only the parameters left after
conditioning. Information criteria compare models of the same response
fitted on the same observations; they do not compare a conditional with
an unconditional likelihood.

## Predictions

`fitted()` and in-sample `predict()` follow the original row order.
Random-effects predictions are marginal over the latent effects.
Fixed-effects predictions for new data add the estimated effects of
known units; unseen units are errors unless `allow.new.levels = TRUE`,
which sets their effect to zero. For the conditional logit, in-sample
fitted values are conditional on each unit's success total, and
new-data probabilities are not identified.

## Computational validation

The test suite (`tests/testthat`) and the scripts in `validation/`
compare each estimator with an established implementation of the same
model:

| Estimator | Reference implementation |
|---|---|
| Pooled GLMs, pooled NB2 | `stats::glm()`, `MASS::glm.nb()` |
| Gaussian pooled, within, between, random; HC1 and cluster covariances | `plm::plm()`, `plm::vcovHC()`, `sandwich` |
| Fixed-effects Poisson and NB2, two-way counts | `fixest`, `pglm` |
| Conditional logit, fixed-effects ordered logit | `survival::clogit()` |
| Random-effects Poisson, NB, binomial | `pglm`, `lme4` |
| Random-effects gamma, beta, ordered | `glmmTMB`, `betareg`, `ordinal::clmm()`, `MASS::polr()` |
| Tobit | `AER::tobit()`, `censReg` |
| Hurdle count part | `pscl::hurdle()` |
| Random slopes | `lme4::lmer()`, `lme4::glmer()`, `glmmTMB`, `GLMMadaptive` |
| IV, Hausman-Taylor | `plm::plm()`, `plm::pht()`, `AER::ivreg()`, `fixest::feols()` |
| Difference and system GMM | `plm::pgmm()` |
| Selection | `stats::glm()`, `plm`, `sandwich`, `sampleSelection::heckit()` (one period) |
| TWFE DiD and event study | `fixest::feols()`, `survival::clogit()` |
| Group-time ATT and aggregations | `did::att_gt()`, `did::aggte()` |
| Extended TWFE | `etwfe::etwfe()`, `etwfe::emfx()` |
| Finite mixtures | `flexmix` |
| Quantile regression | `quantreg::rq()`; MM-QR moment conditions as Stata `xtqreg` |
| Average partial effects | `marginaleffects` |

## Model scope

* Families: Gaussian, Poisson, binomial (logit, probit), NB2, gamma,
  ordered logit and probit, beta and tobit; two-part and hurdle models
  for zeros.
* Fixed effects: Gaussian, Poisson, NB2, gamma, conditional logit and
  ordered logit. There is no fixed-effects estimator for the probit,
  ordered probit, beta and tobit models.
* Random effects: every family; random slopes for Gaussian, Poisson,
  NB2, gamma and binomial models.
* Linear only: instrumental variables (`paniv()`), GMM (`pangmm()`),
  selection (`panselect()`) and quantile regression (`panqr()`).
* Policy: `did()` and `eventstudy()` for Gaussian, count and binary
  outcomes; `attgt()` for continuous outcomes; `etwfe()` for Gaussian,
  Poisson and binary outcomes.

These restrictions keep unlike estimators from being presented under a
common option.
